title: Chat and real-time messaging
summary: Design the delivery path of a chat system: long-lived connections, an ordered store of recent messages, push to phones, an edge cache for big workspaces, per-device encryption and message storage. Read six posts from four companies: WhatsApp 2012 and 2021, Messenger 2014, Slack 2017 and 2020, and Discord 2024. Half are old, and none gives figures for presence or read receipts.

topics.role: Covers pushing updates to a client over a held connection (MQTT, WebSocket) instead of making it ask again. It also covers the gateway that sends websocket dispatches to connected clients.
Describes the ordered queue with one pointer per consumer, so a slow or offline consumer does not stop the others.
Explains choosing a server by hashing, here so that a whole team lands on the same edge cache.
Covers letting a client subscribe only to the events its current view needs, which cut the presence events it receives.
Describes an application-level cache at the edge that answers client queries and shields the backend from reconnecting clients.
Covers splitting one dataset across database shards by a key, here by workspace or by channel.

brief.text: A chat system keeps many phones and browsers connected at once, delivers each message to every device in order, and has to cope with devices that drop off the network and come back. Design the connection layer, the store of recent messages, the push path to the device, the cache that serves big workspaces and the storage under it all. This page does not cover media upload, search, group-call video or typing and read-receipt design. Be careful with the sources: they are from 2012 (WhatsApp), 2014 (Messenger, then run by Facebook), 2017 (Slack, the page shows an update date of June 2020), 2020 (Slack), 2021 (WhatsApp) and 2024 (Discord), from four companies, and each describes its system as of that year. None of them gives figures for presence (who is online), delivery acknowledgements or read receipts. The Slack 2017 post only says that presence updates moved to pub/sub and that clients then received about 5 times fewer presence events. Nothing here says any of the older designs still holds.

requirements.label: 1. Fewer bytes and fewer failed sends
requirements.value: A new sync protocol cut Messenger's non-media data use by about 40% and cut the number of people who hit errors when sending a message by roughly 20% (2014)

requirements.label: 2. Phones go offline
requirements.value: A phone that is offline, or a storage outage, must not stop new messages being accepted. A week of messages is kept for catch-up (2014)

requirements.label: 3. Many connections per machine
requirements.value: One server held over 2 million TCP connections, 2,277,845 open sockets at the time of the post, with plenty of CPU and memory left over (2012)

requirements.label: 4. Connections at the edge
requirements.value: Flannel served 4 million simultaneous connections at peak and 600K client queries per second at the edge (2017)

requirements.label: 5. Very large workspaces
requirements.value: Loading everything at startup became slow once teams reached tens of thousands of users, and an office that reconnects all at once strains the backend (2017)

requirements.label: 6. Small payloads
requirements.value: Messages and deltas should be small on the wire: switching from JSON to Thrift cut the payload by roughly 50% (2014)

requirements.label: 7. Database failures are routine
requirements.value: Hardware failures in the queue's database should be handled in under 30 seconds (2014)

requirements.label: 8. Clients not viewing a server should not get every event
requirements.value: Discord sends clients that are not looking at a server a limited periodic update instead of every message. Its snapshot-style passive update was over 30% of gateway traffic from around 2% of dispatches until it was replaced by a delta (2024)

requirements.label: 9. Several devices per account, still encrypted
requirements.value: In one-on-one chats, a WhatsApp account can use the phone and up to four other nonphone devices at once, with each message encrypted separately for each device and not kept on the server after delivery. Groups still use the Sender Key scheme (2021)

requirements.label: 10. Message storage that spreads load
requirements.value: Slack's datastore served 2.3 million queries per second at peak (2M reads, 300K writes), with a median query latency of 2 ms and p99 of 11 ms, after moving to Vitess (2020)

decisions.question: Your app learns of new data by a light push notification, then sends a complicated HTTPS query and gets a very large JSON reply. Mobile data plans are costly and networks are weak. How should the device stay up to date?

options.label: Keep the pull model but compress the JSON reply and cache the query result on the device
options.why: Smallest change, but every new message still costs a full round trip on a weak network.

options.label: Fetch one snapshot, then subscribe to small delta updates pushed over a light connection and apply them locally
options.why: After the first snapshot the app needs no further queries, but the server must now stream ordered updates.

options.label: Poll the server on a short timer and fetch only the changes since the last poll
options.why: Easy to build, but idle phones still send requests and waste battery and data.

realChoice.text: Messenger moved to a push-based snapshot plus delta model (2014). The client gets an initial snapshot, typically the only HTTPS pull it makes, then subscribes to delta updates that are pushed over MQTT, a low-power, low-bandwidth protocol, as messages arrive. The client applies each delta to its local copy, so it can show an up-to-date view without an HTTPS request. The post says this sync protocol cut non-media data use by about 40%, and that reducing network congestion led to roughly 20% fewer people seeing errors when sending a message.

decisions.question: The deltas travel as JSON. It is flexible and readable, and compression helps, but the wire format is still wasteful. Bytes on a mobile network matter. What do you do about the encoding?

options.label: Stay on JSON and rely on compression, since developers can read it and change it quickly
options.why: Lowest developer overhead, but compression does not fully offset the format's waste.

options.label: Drop messages that are older than a few minutes so fewer bytes are sent in total
options.why: Saves bytes, but users lose messages they were waiting for.

options.label: Move to a compact binary encoding with a schema, accepting less readable traffic
options.why: Smaller on the wire, at the price of tooling and a schema to keep in step on every client.

realChoice.text: Messenger evaluated several replacements for JSON and chose Thrift for messages and delta updates (2014). The post says JSON is good when you need a flexible, human-readable format with little developer overhead, but is not efficient on the wire, and that compression does not entirely make up for it. Switching to Thrift reduced the payload size on the wire by roughly 50%.

decisions.question: One big disk storage tier handles both real-time message delivery and full conversation history. A disk outage or a slow write now delays what the phone sees. How do you split the work?

options.label: Buy faster disks and add more servers to the one storage tier
options.why: Keeps one system, but it still serves two jobs and one slow write still holds up delivery.

options.label: Put an ordered queue in front, with separate pointers for the phone and for the storage tier
options.why: Each side advances at its own pace and can fall behind, but you now run a queue with a bounded backlog.

options.label: Send messages to the phone first and write to disk later from the phone's copy
options.why: Fast delivery, but a lost phone loses a message that never reached storage.

realChoice.text: Messenger built Iris, a totally ordered queue of messaging updates (new messages, read-state changes), with separate pointers for the last update sent to the app and the last one sent to the traditional storage tier (2014). A pointer moves only after a successful send. If the phone is offline or the disk tier is down, its pointer stays still while new messages are still queued and the other pointers advance, so slow disk writes do not hold back real-time delivery. The post describes three tiers by recency: the newest messages go from Iris's memory, a week of messages sits in the queue's backing store, and older history comes from the disk tier.

decisions.question: The queue needs a durable backing store that holds a week of messages, is fast to write and survives a machine failure within seconds. Nothing off the shelf meets all of scale, reliability, speed and flexibility. What do you build it on?

options.label: A new custom storage engine written for this queue alone
options.why: Fits the need exactly, but it is a long project and every bug is yours.

options.label: The existing MySQL on flash, with semi-sync replication so each write is on more than one server
options.why: Reuses known tooling and gains durability across servers, but the database's availability had to be improved first.

options.label: Keep the queue only in memory and rebuild it from the disk tier after a crash
options.why: Fastest writes, but a crash loses the recent messages that are not yet on disk.

realChoice.text: Messenger looked at several existing technologies for the queue's backing store and found none that fit on scale, reliability, speed and flexibility, so it built the queue storage on MySQL and flash (2014). It used semi-sync replication, which gives durability across multiple servers. The post says this lets it handle database hardware failures in under 30 seconds, and that enqueueing a new message is an order of magnitude faster than writing to the traditional disk storage. A message is enqueued once to MySQL and then pushed to apps and to disk in parallel. The post points to a separate talk for the MySQL availability work.

decisions.question: Every user holds a connection open. Do you spread them over many small servers, or tune each server to hold as many connections as it can?

options.label: Many small servers with a few thousand connections each, so one failure affects few users
options.why: Simple to reason about, but the fleet is large and each connection costs more hardware.

options.label: Cap each server at a round number such as 10,000 connections to leave headroom
options.why: Safe margin, but you pay for machines that sit mostly idle.

options.label: Tune the operating system and runtime so one machine holds millions of connections
options.why: Far fewer machines, but it takes OS limits, memory sizing and testing that the defaults do not give you.

realChoice.text: In January 2012 WhatsApp reported pushing its servers to over 2 million TCP connections on one box, after an earlier post about 1 million. The box showed 2,277,845 open sockets, CPU at 37.9% user, 13.6% system and 41.9% idle, and 27G of memory free. It ran FreeBSD 8.2-STABLE on 24 cores of Intel Xeon X5675 with about 103 GB of RAM, with Erlang R14B03 as the runtime. The post lists the tuned limits (for example kern.ipc.maxsockets=2400000 and kern.maxfiles=3000000) and says the load was sustainable. It does not say how many such servers the service ran or how connections were spread across them.

decisions.question: Your client downloads a full snapshot of the workspace at startup: every user, channel, member and recent message. That works for hundreds of people. For tens of thousands it gets slow, and a reconnect after closing a laptop costs almost as much as the first load. What changes?

options.label: Send less at startup and put a cache near the user that answers queries for the rest as they are needed
options.why: Fast to start and cheap to reconnect, but you run a new service and must predict what the client will ask for next.

options.label: Make the backend faster so the full snapshot is built more quickly for every client
options.why: No client change, but each reconnect still costs the backend a full snapshot.

options.label: Cap the workspace size so that no team grows beyond what the full snapshot can handle
options.why: Removes the problem, but turns away the largest customers.

realChoice.text: Slack built Flannel, an application-level cache deployed to its edge points of presence (2017). On connect, Flannel gathers the full startup data, opens a WebSocket to Slack servers in the main AWS region to stay current from real-time events, and gives the client a slimmed-down version. The client then asks Flannel for users and channels on demand, and Flannel pushes data it expects the client to need next. The post says startup data shrank by 7 times on a team of 1.5K users and by 44 times on a team of 32K users. Flannel had been running at the edge since January, serving 4 million simultaneous connections at peak and 600K client queries per second.

decisions.question: You run many cache hosts at the edge. A cache only helps if the data a user needs is already on the host they reach. How should a user be sent to a host?

options.label: Send each connection to the least busy host, so load stays level
options.why: Level load, but teammates land on different hosts and each host caches the same team's data.

options.label: Hash the team and region so that people from the same team in one region reach the same host
options.why: Teammates share one cache, but one big team can make one host busy and adding hosts moves some teams.

options.label: Pin every user to one fixed host for good, chosen when they sign up
options.why: Warm caches, but users cannot move when a host is lost or the network region changes.

realChoice.text: Flannel uses consistent hashing to choose the host a user connects to, so that users on the same team and in the same networking region reach the same Flannel instance, for the best cache efficiency (2017). New or recently disconnected users are then served straight from the Flannel cache, which lowers the impact of reconnect storms on the Slack backend. The post does not say how it handles one very large team landing on a single host.

decisions.question: Every client listens to every event for its team: messages in all its channels, profile updates, presence changes. Most of those events are not relevant to what the user is looking at. How do you cut the traffic?

options.label: Let clients subscribe to only the events the current view needs and change subscriptions when the view changes
options.why: Far fewer events per client, but the server now tracks each client's subscriptions.

options.label: Batch all events into one packet every few seconds and send it to every client
options.why: Fewer packets, but every client still gets every event and live updates become delayed.

options.label: Ask each client to filter on the device and ignore what it does not need
options.why: No server change, but the bytes have already been sent and received.

realChoice.text: Slack said it was moving clients to a pub/sub model, so that a client subscribes to the events that matter in its current view and changes subscriptions when the user switches view (2017). It had already moved user presence updates to pub/sub, and the number of presence events clients received fell by a factor of 5. The post gives no further presence detail, such as how online status is detected or how often it is refreshed. It also lists moving event fanout into Flannel as planned work, not as something finished.

decisions.question: Most members of a very active server are not looking at it. Sending them every message wastes their bandwidth, but they still need a rough view of channels, members and who is in voice. What do you send them?

options.label: Every event, so that all of the clients stay identical to each other at all times
options.why: Simple, but idle clients pay for messages they never read.

options.label: Nothing until they open the server, then a full load of everything the server holds
options.why: Saves bandwidth, but the sidebar goes stale and the first open is slow.

options.label: A periodic update of only what changed, upgrading to the full stream on open
options.why: Cheap for idle clients, but the server must track what each client has already been sent.

realChoice.text: Discord uses passive sessions so clients that may never open a server do not get its messages, and a session is upgraded to a normal one when the user tabs in (2024). Passive sessions still got a periodic update listing channels, members and members in voice. The first version sent all of them even if one element changed. The post says that dispatch was over 30% of gateway traffic while being around 2% of dispatches. Sending only the delta cut it from 35% of gateway bandwidth to 5%, which the post calls a 20% reduction cluster-wide. It does not say how it gets from 35% to 5% to 20%: the drop is 30 percentage points of the gateway's bandwidth, so the 20% figure uses a basis the post does not explain. Together, Passive Sessions v2 and zstandard cut gateway bandwidth by almost 40%. The post notes the snapshot design worked when passive sessions were introduced to scale servers to hundreds of thousands of users. It does not say how online status is detected.

decisions.question: In one-on-one chats, a user now reads on a phone and several other devices, and the server must not be able to read the messages. Who creates the copies for each device, and how long does the server keep them?

options.label: The server keeps one plaintext copy and sends it on to each of the devices
options.why: Cheapest for the sender, but the server can read everything.

options.label: The sender encrypts a copy per device; the server keeps none
options.why: The server never sees content, but the sender does more work as the device count grows.

options.label: One phone stays the source of truth and the other devices only mirror it
options.why: Simple keys, but the other devices are slow and drop whenever the phone is off.

realChoice.text: WhatsApp moved from a phone as the source of truth to independent companion devices (2021), after finding the old design left companions slower and often disconnected when the phone had a poor connection, low battery or was killed by the OS. Each device now has its own identity key, and the server keeps a mapping from account to devices. In one-on-one chats the sending client encrypts and sends the message N times, once per device in the sender's and recipient's device lists; for groups the post says WhatsApp still uses the Sender Key scheme from the Signal Protocol. The post says messages are not stored on the server after they are delivered, and that a companion device gets recent history as an encrypted bundle from the primary device when it is linked. It gives no latency or throughput numbers. It was a limited beta announcement.

decisions.question: All of a workspace's messages and channels sit on one database shard, with thousands of workspaces per shard. The biggest customer makes one shard hot, and a shard outage takes down every customer on it. How do you shard messages?

options.label: Keep sharding by workspace and move the big workspaces to their own hosts
options.why: Small change, but one large workspace's load still lands on a single shard.

options.label: Shard messages by channel, using a layer that splits and routes shards
options.why: Load spreads more evenly, but queries that assumed one workspace per shard must be reworked.

options.label: Keep everything in one large database and buy ever bigger hardware for it
options.why: No routing logic, but there is a limit to one host.

realChoice.text: Slack moved to Vitess, a layer over MySQL, from 2017, and said in December 2020 that it served 99% of query load (2020). The old design sharded by workspace id, which the post says made every customer on a shard feel a shard outage. Slack wanted to shard message data by channel id instead. It considered building the new sharding into the application but found the application too tightly coupled to how data was stored, and said building sharding awareness into the application would not address its operational issues or let it use read replicas more effectively, so it adopted Vitess. In March 2020 query rates rose by 50% in one week and it split a busy keyspace using Vitess. This post is from 2020 and shows nothing about 2021 or later.

inputs.label: Simultaneous connections to hold (Slack reported 4 million at peak, 2017)
Connections per server (WhatsApp reported over 2 million on one box, 2012; your hardware will differ)
Startup data a client downloads before lazy loading (your own number)
Reduction from lazy loading (the post gives 7 times for 1.5K users and 44 times for 32K users)
Non-media data one user's app uses in a month before the change (your own number)
Saving from the new sync protocol (the post says about 40%)
Users with messages in the queue (your own number)
Queued updates per user per day (your own number)
Size of one queued update (your own number)
Devices the sender uses (WhatsApp 2021: the phone plus up to four others)

outputs.label: Servers needed to hold those connections (derived, no spare capacity)
Monthly non-media data after the new sync protocol (derived)
Size of a week of queued updates (derived; the post says a week is kept but gives no size)

Separately encrypted copies the sending client makes for one message in a one-on-one chat (derived; the post says one per device in both lists, we assume the sending device is not counted; groups use Sender Key)

diagram.title: Chat: Messenger's sync path (Iris), Slack's edge cache (Flannel) and datastore (Vitess), Discord's passive sessions and WhatsApp's connection server and device fan-out, each part taken from the post named in its note

nodes.label: Messenger app (snapshot plus deltas)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Messenger post (2014). It pulls one snapshot over HTTPS, then applies deltas pushed over MQTT to its local copy. Less data and fewer requests, but the server must keep an ordered stream for every client.

nodes.label: Iris (ordered queue with pointers)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Messenger post. A totally ordered queue of updates with one pointer for the app and one for the storage tier, so each moves at its own pace. A message is enqueued once and pushed to the app and to disk in parallel. The post does not say how pointers are stored or how a client catches up beyond the week kept.

nodes.label: Queue backing store (MySQL on flash, semi-sync)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Messenger post. Holds a week of messages. Semi-sync replication gives durability across servers and database hardware failures are handled in under 30 seconds. The post does not describe the replica layout.

nodes.label: Traditional disk storage tier
nodes.tradeoff: From the Messenger post. Serves older conversation history and full inbox snapshot fetches. Disk writes are slow, which is why they are kept off the real-time path.

nodes.label: Slack client (WebSocket, lazy loading)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Flannel post (2017). It loads minimal data at startup, keeps a WebSocket for real-time events and asks the edge for users and channels as needed. The page's own reading: the first lookup of anything not yet loaded needs a query.

nodes.label: Team-affinity routing (consistent hashing)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Flannel post. Users on the same team and in the same networking region are sent to the same Flannel instance for cache efficiency. The post does not say how an oversized team is balanced.

nodes.label: Flannel (edge application cache)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Flannel post. Caches users, channels and bots at the edge and answers client queries, and pushes data it expects the client to need. Reconnecting clients are served from it, not from the backend. The post lists event fanout in Flannel as planned, not done.

nodes.label: Slack servers in the main AWS region
nodes.tradeoff: From the Flannel post. Flannel opens a WebSocket here to consume real-time events and loads the full startup data. The post says the message server currently forwards a copy to Flannel for each connected user.

nodes.label: Presence updates (pub/sub)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Flannel post. Presence moved to a subscription model and clients received about 5 times fewer presence events. The post says nothing about where the broker runs or how online status is detected.

nodes.label: Connection server (FreeBSD, Erlang)
nodes.tradeoff: From the WhatsApp post (2012). One tuned machine held over 2 million TCP connections with CPU 41.9% idle. The post gives no detail of what the server does with a message, how many servers there were or how they connect to the other parts drawn here, so no link is drawn.

nodes.label: Discord passive sessions
nodes.tradeoff: From the Discord post (2024). Clients not viewing a server get a periodic limited update instead of every message and are upgraded when they open it. The first version sent full snapshots; the delta version cut that traffic from 35% of gateway bandwidth to 5%. The post does not describe presence detection.

nodes.label: WhatsApp client fan-out per device
nodes.tradeoff: From the WhatsApp 2021 post. In one-on-one chats the sending client encrypts one copy per device in both device lists (groups still use Sender Key), and messages are not stored on the server after delivery. More work for the sender as devices grow; the post gives no timings.

nodes.label: Vitess keyspaces (sharded MySQL)
nodes.tradeoff: From the Slack 2020 post. Message data was meant to shard by channel id, not workspace id, to spread load. Served 2.3 million queries per second at peak with p99 11 ms. The post says that under the old workspace sharding, a shard outage meant a full outage for every customer on it.

failures.label: A phone goes offline for a while
The disk storage tier has an outage or very slow writes
Hardware under the queue's MySQL fails
A whole office loses its network and its clients reconnect at once

compare:
These are six posts from four companies across 2012 to 2024, so read them as separate snapshots, not one system. WhatsApp is from January 2012 and July 2021, Messenger from October 2014 (when it was part of Facebook), Slack from May 2017 (the page shows an update date of June 2020) and December 2020, and Discord from September 2024. Each describes its system as of that year. Nothing here says the older designs still hold today. The posts do not say how WhatsApp's connection servers hand messages on, so the diagram draws no link from them, and it draws no links between products. There are still no figures here for presence or read receipts, so this page does not size them.

The older posts attack different ends of the same path. WhatsApp shows what one machine can hold: over 2 million connections with CPU to spare, but it says nothing about the messages on them. Messenger works on the middle: an ordered queue with a pointer per consumer lets a phone or a disk tier fall behind without blocking the other, and the price is a queue with a one-week backlog, backed by MySQL on flash. Slack works on the edge: it sends less at startup and keeps a cache near the user, and the price is a new service that has to guess what the client will ask for next. The newer posts add three more ends of the path. Discord cuts what idle clients receive: its passive update went from full snapshots to deltas, and the post says the snapshot design worked until servers grew larger. WhatsApp 2021 puts the cost of encryption on the sender, which encrypts one copy per device, in exchange for a server that keeps no message after delivery. Slack 2020 spreads storage load by sharding message data by channel instead of workspace, at the price of reworking queries written for one workspace per shard.

The common move is to stop sending everything to everyone. Messenger sends a snapshot once and then deltas. Slack sends a slim startup payload (7 times smaller for 1.5K users, 44 times for 32K) and then fills in on demand, and has moved presence to subscriptions. Each post also names its limit. Messenger's gains are measured in data use (about 40%) and send errors (roughly 20%), not in delivery latency. Slack's fanout and further pub/sub work were still plans in the post. WhatsApp's figure is for a single box, not a fleet.

quiz.question: Why does Iris keep a separate pointer for the app and for the storage tier?
options: Each side moves at its own pace, so a slow disk cannot stall delivery
It lets the phone write straight to the disk tier after it confirms a message
It keeps two copies of every message so one copy is always available
quiz.why: A pointer advances only after a successful send. If the phone is offline or the disk is down, its pointer stays while new messages are still queued and the other pointers advance.
wrong: The queue writes to disk, not the app.
The pointers mark positions in one queue, not two copies.

quiz.question: Why did Messenger move from pull to a snapshot plus pushed deltas?
options: Pushed deltas mean the server no longer has to keep any message history at all
After one snapshot the app stays current with no more HTTPS queries
MQTT guarantees that no delta is ever lost between server and phone
quiz.why: The old way needed a complex HTTPS query and a large JSON reply for each push notification. The new way applies small deltas to a local copy, and non-media data use fell by about 40%.
wrong: The queue still keeps a week of messages.
The post calls MQTT low-power and low-bandwidth, and does not make a delivery guarantee.

quiz.question: What does Slack's use of consistent hashing in Flannel aim for?
options: Spreading each team's users evenly across every host in their whole region
Sending one team's users in a region to one host for a warm cache
Choosing the host that is geographically nearest to each single user
quiz.why: Users of one team in the same networking region reach the same Flannel instance, which gives the best cache efficiency and serves reconnecting users from cache.
wrong: Spreading teams out would split the cache.
The post names team and region, not distance to each user.

quiz.question: What did Slack report after moving presence updates to pub/sub?
options: Presence events fell by about 40% and send errors fell with them
The post gives no figure, only that presence now uses subscriptions
Clients got about 5 times fewer presence events
quiz.why: The post says the number of presence events received by clients was reduced by a factor of 5. It gives no detail on how presence is detected.
wrong: The 40% figure belongs to Messenger's data use.
It does give a figure, a factor of 5.

quiz.question: What does Flannel's edge cache do for the Slack backend when many clients reconnect?
options: It serves them from its cache
It queues the reconnecting clients until the backend has capacity
It sends every reconnecting client a full snapshot of the team
quiz.why: New or recently disconnected users are served directly from Flannel's cache, which reduces the impact of reconnect storms on backend servers.
wrong: The post describes serving from cache, not queueing.
A full snapshot is what the old model did, and Flannel slims it down.

quiz.question: What did Discord change to cut the cost of passive sessions?
options: It stopped sending passive sessions anything at all
It sent only the changes since the last update
It moved passive sessions to a different protocol
quiz.why: The post says the old update resent all channels, members and members in voice even if one element changed. The delta version cut it from 35% of gateway bandwidth to 5%.
wrong: Passive sessions still get a periodic update.
The post's change is to the content of the update.

quiz.question: In WhatsApp's 2021 multi-device design, who encrypts a one-on-one message for each recipient device?
options: The server, which holds the plaintext until delivery
The sending client, once per device
The recipient's phone, which then forwards a copy to the other devices
quiz.why: In one-on-one chats the sending client encrypts and transmits it N times, and messages are not stored on the server after delivery. Groups still use Sender Key.
wrong: The server cannot read the messages in this design.
The phone is no longer the source of truth.
